scenario: AITA for massaging my guy friend in front of his girlfriend? | I (32F) met my friend (30M) at work last year. We both quit our jobs and became close friends, he introduced me straight away to his girlfriend and this girl is a gem. We hang out a lot the three of us and I love both of them now, even if I knew him first. Today, we were hanging out at the beach for the fireworks and my guy friend was in a bad mood. I asked him what was wrong and he said he had a bad headache. I asked him if he wanted me to give him a head massage because I usually give massages to my friends & family. However, he's pretty tall so I couldn't give it to him while sitting. He then put his head on my laps and I was massaging his head while talking to his girlfriend. I didn't realise it was an uncomfortable situation before seeing the girlfriend's face, which was a bit sceptical. I then quickly put an end to it and sat back at my place. I'm scared I made her mad, even if she was super nice to me the rest of the evening, I find myself completely stupid for not realising it would be super awkward. By the way, I'm dating someone else and I often tell them about my dates and all, so there is absolutely no ambiguity between me & him, and I always see them together, they're a package and I love it. Was I being an asshole here?

Thanksgiving is next week and I'm responsible for preparing the turkey for the first time. My family has a specific recipe for it that everyone expects. How would you approach that?

Preparing your family’s Thanksgiving turkey for the first time can feel daunting, but with a structured approach, you can ensure success while staying true to tradition. Here’s a step-by-step guide to help you navigate the process with confidence: --- ### **1. Review the Recipe Thoroughly** - **Clarify details**: Ask a family member to confirm the exact recipe (e.g., brining method, seasoning, cooking time, temperature, and any special techniques like butter basting or herb stuffing). - **Check for notes**: Look for handwritten instructions, family traditions (e.g., "always add a splash of bourbon" or "let it rest for 30 minutes"), or adjustments (e.g., "reduce salt if using salted butter"). - **Gather tools**: Ensure you have all necessary equipment (meat thermometer, roasting pan, basting brush, etc.). --- ### **2. Plan Ahead (Critical for First-Timers!)** - **Buy the turkey early**: Fresh turkeys sell out quickly. Opt for a **whole turkey (12–14 lbs for 6–8 people)** or a **brined turkey (10–12 lbs)** if your recipe includes brining. Frozen turkeys require more thawing time (about 24 hours per 4–5 lbs in the fridge). - **Thawing**: If frozen, thaw in the fridge (not on the counter) starting **3–4 days before cooking**. Use the "day-by-day" thawing guide: - **Day 1**: Start thawing (e.g., a 12-lb turkey needs ~3 days). - **Day 2–3**: Continue thawing; check for ice buildup. - **Day before cooking**: Ensure it’s fully thawed (liquid should run clear). - **Prep workspace**: Clean and organize your kitchen, tools, and ingredients the day before. --- ### **3. Follow the Recipe Step-by-Step** Here’s a general framework based on common family recipes (adjust for specifics): #### **A. Brining (If Applicable)** - **Why**: Brining (soaking in saltwater) keeps the turkey juicy. If your recipe includes this, start **24–48 hours before cooking**. - **How**: - Dissolve **1 cup salt + ¼ cup sugar** per gallon of water (or use a pre-made brine). - Add **aromatics** (e.g., garlic, herbs, citrus peels) if the recipe specifies. - Submerge the turkey in a **large container** (use a weight to keep it submerged). - **Rinse before cooking** and pat dry. #### **B. Pre-Cooking Prep** - **Dry the turkey thoroughly**: Pat it dry with paper towels to ensure even browning. - **Seasoning**: - **Inside cavity**: Rub with butter, herbs (thyme, rosemary, sage), garlic, and salt/pepper as per the recipe. - **Outside**: Season generously with salt, pepper, and any other spices (e.g., sage, black peppercorn). - **Stuffing (if used)**: - Prepare stuffing **ahead** (day before) and refrigerate. - Stuff loosely into the cavity (overstuffing can dry it out). Some families prefer **separate stuffing** baked in a dish. #### **C. Roasting** - **Oven setup**: - Preheat oven to **325°F (165°C)**—lower temps ensure even cooking. - Place turkey **breast-side up** on a rack in a roasting pan (for airflow). - Add **liquid** (water, broth, or apple juice) to the pan to prevent drying. - **Basting**: - Baste every **45–60 minutes** with pan juices or melted butter/herb mixture (if the recipe calls for it). - **Butter basting**: Melt butter with herbs, spoon over turkey periodically. - **Cooking time**: - **Unbrined turkey**: ~13–15 minutes per pound (e.g., 12 lbs = ~2 hours). - **Brined turkey**: ~10–12 minutes per pound (e.g., 10 lbs = ~2 hours). - **Estimated total time**: 3–4 hours (including rest time). - **Thermometer check**: - Insert a **meat thermometer** into the thickest part of the thigh (avoid bone). - **Safe temp**: **165°F (74°C)** in the thickest part of the thigh and breast. - **Don’t overcook**: Turkeys continue cooking while resting (see below). #### **D. Resting (Non-Negotiable!)** - **Why**: Letting the turkey rest redistributes juices for moist meat. - **How**: - Tent loosely with foil and let rest **30–45 minutes** before carving. - Keep warm in the oven (turn off heat) or on a warming tray. --- ### **4. Carving and Serving** - **Carve at the table**: Use a sharp knife to slice against the grain. - **Serve with pan juices**: Strain and reduce juices for gravy if your recipe includes it. - **Leftovers**: Store in airtight containers (e.g., turkey, stuffing, gravy) within 2 hours of cooking. --- ### **5. Troubleshooting Common Issues** | **Problem** | **Solution** | |---------------------------|-----------------------------------------------| | Turkey dries out | Brine it, baste often, or use a meat thermometer. | | Skin doesn’t brown | Broil for 2–3 minutes at the end (watch closely!). | | Stuffing gets soggy | Bake stuffing separately or stuff loosely. | | Overcooked | Remove from oven at 155°F (thigh) and rest. | | Turkey too salty | Rinse before cooking if brining; use unsalted butter. | --- ### **6. Pro Tips for First-Timers** - **Delegate**: Ask a family member to help with basting or carving. - **Set reminders**: Use phone alarms for basting intervals and thermometer checks. - **Document**: Take photos of each step to compare with the recipe later. - **Stay calm**: If something goes wrong (e.g., oven temp fluctuates), focus on the thermometer, not the clock. --- ### **7. Family-Specific Adjustments** If your family’s recipe includes unique elements (e.g.,: - **Herb butter**: Melt butter with herbs and rub under the skin. - **Apple cider brine**: Use apple cider instead of water for a subtle sweetness. - **Dry-brine**: Salt the turkey 1–2 days before cooking (no liquid brine). - **Herb stuffing**: Use a mix of celery, onions, breadcrumbs, and herbs. ), double-check these details with a family member. --- ### **8. Timeline Example (For a 12-lb Turkey)** | **Day Before** | **Morning Of** | **Cooking Day** | |--------------------------|-------------------------------|-------------------------------------| | Brine turkey (if needed) | Thaw turkey (if frozen) | Preheat oven to 325°F. | | Prep stuffing | Dry turkey, season | Place turkey in oven. | | | | Baste every 45 mins. | | | | Check temp at ~1.5 hours (155°F). | | | | Rest 30–45 mins before carving. | --- ### **Final Encouragement** You’ve got this! The key is to **follow the recipe closely**, **use a thermometer**, and **let the turkey rest**. Even if it’s not perfect, the love and effort will shine through. If you’re unsure about any step, don’t hesitate to ask for help—family traditions are meant to be shared.   - Noticed her body language sooner and adjusted.

The key takeaway: **Always check in with everyone in the room** before assuming what’s comfortable.
